What gets me about this sort of accusation is how reductive it is. Ignoring the fact that much of the allegations are false, just for the sole purpose of making this post somewhat succinct, any person with a reasonable amount of scientific and academic literacy should be willing to recognize that many situations in a wider group are a likely the result of countless major and minor factors that ultimately influence the situation into whatever form it takes. To point at any one factor as the sole cause is simply a sign of poor education and lacking scientific literacy. If racism is a factor in the glut of medieval European fantasies that clutter game shelves, then it is very likely a minor one. There are a number of what anyone who knows the entertainment and gaming industries would recognize as more pertinent factors, which would make for an altogether more realistic picture than pointing solely to any sort of racism.

First of all, what are the cultures the majority of these games are made in? Overwhelmingly European or Anglo-American influenced cultures. Given that much of our modern conception of the fantasy genre was modeled on the myths and legends of medieval Europe, these themes are familiar to the average English-speaking consumer. They'll know perfectly well what you mean when you start talking about dwarves, but mention a Gumiho in front of them and watch them draw a blank. Given that the economic and technological condition required to maintain a profitable games industry is mainly endemic to Western Europe and the Anglo-American sphere, it makes sense that a large part of this could just be due to people working from a cultural background that both they and the average consumer are likely to understand.

Secondly, there is a general precedent for this sort of milieu already embedded within the collective consciousness of the games industry. Role-Playing was invented as a recreational medium due to the influence of DnD, which was largely informed by the same vein of Tolkeinesque fantasy that produced the vast majority of the literary fantasy canon. The earliest computer role-playing games were basically electronic adaptions of both DnD and the various fantasy RPGs that sprung up when DnD proved that RPGs could be a workable medium. We've been working in the Tolkien imitation mode for so long that even the most creatively bankrupt of developers know that set of ideas well enough to build a game utilizing them, and when budgets are tight and development costs can be truly astronomical, the familiar and cliche is much more workable than the exotic.

And while we're on the subject of money, can we talk a bit about how the industry works? This set of ideas about what fantasy is continues for the same reason that Hollywood allegedly pumps out nothing but remakes or adaptions every single year. The creative people may be the ones who have to create and furnish the concept, but they are at the mercy of various executives and businessmen who are duty-bound to look after the bottom line above all else. In fact, it's arguably even worse than Hollywood, because the cost of your average triple-A game far outstrips your average Hollywood blockbuster, due to both the technology that has to be worked with and the stupendous number of people that are involved in the making and distribution of your average triple-A release. When the money-men are charged with working under those kind of conditions, they are going to become very risk-averse, simply because of the fact that any risk that doesn't pan out is going to lead to heavy losses for their superiors numbered Cayman Islands bank accounts. Under those kinds of conditions, why bother doing anything other than what you know is going to sell enough units to break even at least. This conception of Fantasy is so common in the games industry because the money-men know that it won't alienate consumers, therefore leading to heavy financial losses.

Ultimately, a large part of this is very likely due to a familiarity with that milieu making it workable to the creatively bankrupt, known to consumers, and a great benefit to the executives looking out for the company bottom line. If you want something other than what the mainstream pumps out day by day, then you have to vote with your wallet. Buy original games from independent creators working outside the ISO Standard Fantasy Template, buy games from triple-A studios that dare go outside the norm, buy every noble experiment in thematic diversity. That way, you make a risky quantity into a known aspect and show creators that there is a market for games outside that template, and that there is enough money to be made from these diversions to keep the bottom line happy. Just crying 'racism' every time the industry does not contort itself to your liking is not only conceited, it is a veiled threat to those creators who can't introduce more diversity due to the simple fact that any thematic diversion is a risk to the bottom line. The rebel campaign may bring attention from the industry at large, but none of that means a thing if you aren't willing to keep those diversions alive and show the executives that diversity is not anathema to your bottom line and people are willing to buy games that fall outside the comfortable norm.
